title: Object & Blob Storage
summary: Storing large, infrequently-updated files outside the database, and wiring uploads without proxying bytes through your servers.

slides.markdown:
**Object storage** (S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob) is a separate system built specifically for large, mostly-immutable files — images, videos, backups, exports — that would be a poor fit inside a relational database.

The standard pattern is a split: **metadata in the database, bytes in the object store**, connected by a URL or key. This topic covers why that split exists and how uploads work without your app servers ever touching the actual file bytes.

slides.sectionTitle: What object storage is for: large, immutable, infrequently-updated blobs
slides.markdown:
**Object storage** stores each file as an opaque blob addressed by a key, with no concept of directories, no partial updates, and typically no strong transactional guarantees — you replace a whole object, you don't patch three bytes in the middle of it. In exchange, it's built to hold effectively unlimited data cheaply, replicated across multiple availability zones for durability (S3, for example, is designed for 99.999999999% durability), and served directly over HTTP.

That trade — no partial updates, no directory structure — is exactly right for the files it's meant for: a profile photo, a video upload, a nightly backup. These are written once (or rarely), read many times, and never need a byte-level patch.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: upload flow — client, app, object store, CDN
slides.markdown:
![Sequence diagram: client requests a pre-signed URL from the app server, uploads bytes directly to the object store, then the app server records metadata; a CDN sits in front of the object store for downloads](assets/presigned-upload-flow.svg)

The app server appears twice in this flow but never once in the middle of the file transfer itself — it issues a pre-signed URL, then later records metadata once the upload completes. The actual bytes travel directly between the client and the object store.

A CDN in front of the object store handles downloads the same way: it caches and serves the bytes close to the reader, without routing every download through the app tier either.

slides.sectionTitle: Object storage vs a database BLOB column vs a filesystem
slides.markdown:
| | Object storage | Database BLOB column | Local filesystem |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scale | Effectively unlimited, cheap per GB | Bloats the database, expensive to back up | Limited by one machine's disk |
| Durability | Built-in multi-AZ replication | Only as durable as your DB backups | Lost if the machine dies, unless mirrored |
| Serving large files | Direct HTTP, CDN-friendly | Must proxy through the app and DB | Must proxy through the app |
| Best for | Large, infrequently-updated files | Small blobs tightly coupled to a row's transaction | Ephemeral/temp files on one host |

**How to decide:** default to object storage for anything larger than a few KB or accessed by URL; keep the database for the metadata that describes it, and only use a BLOB column for small binary data that must be transactionally consistent with the row it belongs to.

slides.sectionTitle: Metadata in the DB, bytes in the object store: the standard split
slides.markdown:
The database stores everything that's small and needs to be queried — a file's owner, upload time, size, content type, and the object store **key** that points to the actual bytes. The object store holds only the bytes themselves, addressed by that key.

This split lets each system do its job: the database indexes and joins metadata fast ("all photos uploaded by this user this month") without ever touching gigabytes of image data, and the object store serves large files efficiently without needing to understand rows, joins, or query planning. Losing this split — say, storing a file path as a fragile local filesystem path instead of an object key — is what makes migrations to a new storage backend painful later.

slides.sectionTitle: Pre-signed URLs: uploading/downloading without proxying through your servers
slides.markdown:
A **pre-signed URL** is a time-limited, cryptographically signed URL that grants temporary permission to upload or download one specific object, without the requester needing the object store's actual credentials. Your app server generates it (using credentials it does hold) and hands it to the client, which then talks to the object store directly.

This matters for scale: without pre-signed URLs, every file upload would stream through your app server first, doubling bandwidth cost and tying up an app-server connection for the whole upload. With them, the app server's job shrinks to "issue a short-lived permission slip and record metadata after," and the actual bytes never touch your infrastructure.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: storing large binary files directly in a relational database
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "It's simpler to keep everything in one database — let's store uploaded images as BLOB columns alongside the rest of the row."

**Why it's wrong:** large BLOBs bloat table and index size, slow down backups and replication (since the whole file is copied every time, even for logically unrelated schema changes), and force every read of that row's other columns to potentially load megabytes of binary data the query never asked for.

**Correct model:** store the file in object storage and keep only a reference (key, size, content type) in the database row. The database stays small and fast to query and back up; the object store handles what it's actually built for — serving large files cheaply and durably.

slides.sectionTitle: Multipart upload: splitting a large file into independently-retryable chunks
slides.markdown:
Uploading a single 5GB video as one HTTP request is fragile: any network blip partway through means restarting the entire transfer from byte zero. **Multipart upload** splits the file into independent chunks, commonly 5-100MB each, uploaded separately (often in parallel), with the object store assembling them into the final object once every part has arrived and been acknowledged.

If part 14 of 60 fails, only that one chunk needs retrying, not the whole 5GB file — for a slow or flaky connection, this is the difference between an upload that eventually succeeds and one that never completes. It also lets a client upload multiple chunks concurrently over separate connections, often finishing faster than one large sequential transfer would.

Most object store SDKs switch to multipart automatically past a size threshold (S3's is commonly triggered above 100MB), so an application rarely has to hand-roll this — but understanding the mechanism explains why very large uploads behave so differently from small ones under a flaky network.

slides.sectionTitle: The consistency nuance: can you read an object right after you wrote it?
slides.markdown:
Object stores historically didn't guarantee that a read immediately following a write would see the new data — older S3 documentation described eventual consistency for overwrites of an existing key, meaning a client re-reading a key it just updated could briefly get stale bytes, especially across regions or through a CDN cache in front of the store. Modern S3 (since December 2020) provides strong read-after-write consistency for all operations, but plenty of other object stores, and CDN layers sitting in front of any of them, still don't.

This matters concretely: a service that writes a new profile photo, then immediately generates a thumbnail by reading that same object back, can occasionally process the *old* photo if the store or a caching layer in the path hasn't caught up yet. The defensive pattern is to pass the freshly-written object's own bytes (or a version/ETag) directly to the next step in the pipeline, rather than re-reading by key and trusting it reflects the write that just happened.

The senior-level habit here: never assume a storage layer's consistency model without checking it, and design any read-after-write-dependent pipeline to route data forward explicitly rather than round-tripping through a re-read.
